meaning: A place on the ledger that holds XRP and tokens, identified by an address starting with r.
The transaction that changes an account's settings and flags.
An account's public identifier, 25 to 35 characters starting with r.
NOSHASHI's process of checking something against rules and returning a verdict.
A change to the XRPL's rules, enabled after 80% of validators support it for two weeks.
A server that has not upgraded when an amendment activates, and stops following the ledger.
Anti-Money-Laundering: rules to stop criminal money moving.
Automated market maker: a pool of two assets that trades automatically (XLS-30).
A seat in an AMM pool that gives its holder discounted trading for a time.
Routing a token-to-token trade through XRP when that gives a better price.
An account nobody can sign for again: master key disabled, regular key unusable, no signer list.
A check whose failure gives NO-GO.
The server call that returns an order book's offers.
A crypto (or virtual) asset service provider: a regulated business handling digital assets.
A deferred payment the receiver cashes when they choose.
An issuer power to take tokens back from a holder. Must be enabled before any trust lines exist (XLS-39).
A ledger that has stopped taking transactions but is not yet validated.
Following the laws and rules that apply to moving money.
NOSHASHI's read-only interface for verdicts and readings.
How much of an asset or activity sits with a few parties; measured with the HHI.
How validators agree on the next ledger without mining.
Whoever is on the other side of a transaction.
An on-ledger proof that an account passed a check (XLS-70).
A token's name, 3 characters or 40 hex. Anyone can use any code, so it proves nothing alone.
A freeze where the holder can neither send nor receive the token (XLS-77).
The amount a payment actually delivered, in its metadata. The figure to credit.
How much is on offer in an order book.
A number telling a shared account which customer a payment is for.
Proof that an account belongs to a website: the site lists the account in its /.well-known/xrp-ledger.toml.
The decentralised exchange built into the XRPL.
A fixed-length fingerprint of data. Change anything and the digest changes completely.
A web domain an account claims, verifiable against a file on that domain.
The smallest unit of XRP: 1 XRP = 1,000,000 drops.
Funds locked until a time passes or a condition is met.
The transaction that releases a matured escrow. Nothing pays out until someone submits it.
An approved, recorded override of a NO-GO for a stated reason.
How high transaction costs are running because the network is busy.
An on/off setting on an account or trust line.
A control where a second person must approve a change.
An issuer power to stop a holder sending its token on.
Depth backed by owners who can actually deliver.
The server call that returns an issuer's obligations.
An issuer freezing every holder of its tokens at once.
A verdict meaning every check passed.
A transaction's or object's 64-character hexadecimal identifier.
A log where each entry includes the fingerprint of the previous one, so edits show.
Herfindahl-Hirschman Index: the sum of squared percentage shares; 10,000 is total concentration.
A verdict meaning a person should review before moving.
NOSHASHI's small live panel in the macOS menu bar.
A check state meaning the ledger did not give enough to decide. Never a pass.
A case in NOSHASHI collecting verdicts, readings and notes, with a hash-chained log.
Another name for an issued token: a promise from its issuer.
The account that creates a token and sets its rules.
Know Your Customer: verifying who a customer is.
One numbered snapshot of the whole XRPL, produced every 3 to 5 seconds.
A ledger's number. Fixes a reading to a moment anyone can re-check.
The most of a token you are willing to hold on a trust line.
All the depth shown on a book, including offers nobody can fill.
A token received for adding assets to an AMM pool; carries a fee vote.
The real, live XRP Ledger, as opposed to test networks.
An account's original key pair. It can be disabled.
The record of what a transaction actually did, attached once it is validated.
The EU's regulation for crypto-assets, including stablecoin issuers.
The average of the best bid and best ask.
Several keys signing together, set with a signer list.
A unique token (XLS-20). Its ID encodes the rights its issuer kept.
The 64-character identifier of an NFT, which encodes its flags.
A permanent promise by an issuer never to freeze.
A verdict meaning a blocking check failed.
A check state meaning the check does not apply.
The total of an issuer's tokens held by others: its real circulating supply.
NOSHASHI's agent mode that watches for changes and opens investigations.
An order posted on the DEX to trade one asset for another.
All the offers for one trading pair.
XRP locked for each object an account owns, such as a trust line or offer.
A payment whose Amount is only a maximum; it can deliver less and still succeed.
NOSHASHI's signed, portable record of an asset's posture.
A route that lets a payment convert currencies on the way.
Many small off-ledger payments settled later in one transaction.
An area where only accounts with the right credentials may take part (XLS-80).
An organisation's own thresholds and rules applied to verdicts.
Where an account came from: its age and first funder.
The minimum total signing weight needed to act for an account.
NOSHASHI's record of a verdict: ledger index, rules version, checks and digest.
A second key an account nominates to sign for it.
An issuer setting: you need its approval to hold its token.
XRP an account must keep locked: a base reserve plus an owner reserve per object.
Decoding a transaction before signing it, to see what it really does. Most thefts start with a signature the owner did not understand.
A check state meaning a human decision is needed.
Proving a credential exists without revealing the personal data behind it.
An account's transaction counter, starting at its creation ledger index.
The keys and weights used for multi-signature.
The gap between the best bid and the best ask.
A token meant to hold a steady value, such as one US dollar.
The field book_offers adds when an owner cannot cover an offer.
A result prefix: failed, but recorded and the fee charged.
The success result. It does not mean the full Amount arrived.
An asset on the XRPL other than XRP, created by an issuer.
A signed instruction that changes the ledger.
The small XRP fee each transaction pays, which is destroyed.
A percentage (0% to 100%) an issuer charges when holders send its token to each other.
FATF Recommendation 16: sender and receiver details travel with transfers above a threshold.
The link you open to an issuer to hold its token.
Unique Node List: the validators a server trusts not to collude.
An offer still listed although its owner cannot fill it.
A ledger at least 80% of trusted validators agreed on. It is final.
A server that votes on which ledger is the true next one.
A check whose failure gives HOLD rather than NO-GO.
A signed notification NOSHASHI sends to your own system when an event happens.
An address format that packs an address and destination tag together.
A numbered proposal for a new XRPL standard, such as XLS-30 for AMMs.
The XRP Ledger's own currency.
The XRP Ledger.
Sending someone a tiny payment from a lookalike address, matching the start and end of one they use, so they copy it from their history by mistake.
The transaction that deletes an account and sends its remaining XRP to another; thieves use it to sweep throwaway accounts.
Showing, from the ledger, the XRP an institution holds in the accounts it names for its customers.
A tree of hashes and sums over customer balances whose root proves the total without revealing any balance.
The path from one customer's leaf to the published root, which proves their balance is counted.
Reserves divided by published customer liabilities; 100% or more means fully backed.
XRP set aside to make customers whole up to a per-customer limit, secured only if no single key can move it.
Checking an outbound payment before it is signed: will it bounce, and is the destination new, a lookalike, sanctioned or reported.
Addresses reported by institutions with transaction evidence and confirmed by an independent reviewer.
Orders placed and replaced again and again without filling; it makes an order book look deeper than it is.
NOSHASHI's list of unsigned transactions that make an account harder to take over, for the owner to sign in their own wallet.
NOSHASHI's plain-text record of a theft trail and recovery paths, with a SHA-256 fingerprint anyone can re-check.
The secret an account's keys are derived from. Whoever has it controls the account; no legitimate service ever asks for it.
NOSHASHI's Strategic alert: a signed security_alert webhook when a watched account's keys change or it is deleted.
